$schema_note: ONE definition of which guards publish a verdict, read by both languages.
Python publishes from ETL/lib/guard_verdicts.py (the weekly cron drives it);
TypeScript from web/scripts/guardVerdict.ts. mandate/health/check.py reads
this list and raises the ONE 'Mandate health' issue when a verdict is red or
late. Collapsed to five guards on 2026-11-10 (Phase 0); the rest protected
the retired one-pager brief and are archived at archive/2026-11-pre-pivot.
Fields:
id        the verdict's key. Stable; renaming one loses its history.
cadence   'weekly'    the ETL cron publishes it, so it can be LATE:
SILENT is enforced against the observed spacing.
'on_change' a credentialled run publishes it. It has no clock to
be late against, so SILENT is not enforced. It goes
red two other ways: DRIFTED when the code it judges
changes, and STALE when the CORPUS moves past it.
needs     what the guard cannot run without, and LOAD-BEARING: a guard
that names a store here is answering a question about DATA, so
its verdict is void once the corpus moves, whatever its cadence.
Three of the four on_change guards judge live Postgres and no
fingerprinted file changes when a call closes, so without this
their verdicts would have covered today's corpus forever.
Derived from, not duplicated -- do not add a 'reads_corpus' flag
that can disagree with the credentials the guard actually needs.
code      repo-relative paths whose content the verdict is bound to. A
verdict produced against a different hash of these is DRIFTED.
For a weekly guard this is what makes 'the container is running
last week's code' visible; for an on_change guard it is the
whole enforcement mechanism.
refresh   the exact command that produces a fresh verdict. Printed in the
failure, because a guard that says 'stale' without saying how to
fix it gets muted.
command   present only where ETL/lib/guard_verdicts.py drives the guard
and publishes for it. A guard that publishes its OWN verdict
(the TypeScript ones do, because they have real figures to
carry) has no command here: two ways to publish one verdict is
two things to keep in step.
tolerate  exit codes that mean 'worth saying out loud, not worth failing
over'. Named per guard, never inferred from the number.
code_suffixes  narrows what a named directory contributes to the hash.

$why: Where a reader without credentials gets the verdicts. The site already
holds DATABASE_URL because the product cannot work without it; that is a
credential we cannot avoid having. A DATABASE_URL secret in GitHub
Actions is one we can, and it would widen a compromised workflow from
'can read our code' to 'can read and write every award we hold'.
Override with GUARD_FEED_URL to point at a preview deployment or a local
`next dev`; nothing in an automatic path may need that override.

guards.why: What the ETL corpus contains, and how the run that produced it went. Everything below is judged against the newest one.

Every table and column in the store must be creatable from committed DDL, and present. When there were two stores, the volume's funding_instruments had no `tier` while the laptop's did, and because the census reads `tier` a missing COLUMN was reported for half a day as a coverage LOSS. Since 2026-11-05 there is one store (schema capital); it runs on the cron because it is a question about the LIVE store, which CI holds no credentials for.
A country's offerable inventory falling with no corresponding corpus change. Already a cron step; publishing its verdict is what makes the result readable without credentials.

Did the run that built this corpus finish every step it started. The other guards ask what the corpus CONTAINS and whether its schema is right; a half-refreshed corpus answers both perfectly well, and the coverage gate passed three censuses in a row that describe runs which failed. The outcome of a run is a property of the corpus that run produced, and it was being kept in a different store from the corpus -- so it did not survive `make pull-db`, and a partial volume became a publishable-looking laptop corpus with nothing left to say otherwise. The mark lives in the store itself, beside the rows it describes.

No published `who may apply` block may state a population that cannot apply. Five did when this guard was found on 2026-08-08: two Latvian guarantee schemes the borrower's bank submits, an Innovasjon Norge row whose text was a cluster-programme paragraph its own recorded source never asserted, a closed English risk-finance scheme delivered through financial intermediaries, and an Irish community scheme applied for by registered project coordinators. A founder matched on any of them spends the effort and is rejected at the end, which is worse than never being shown the fund. It says FAILS THE BUILD in its own header and had been wired into nothing since the day it was written.
